questions.q: Which of the following is a non-luminous object?
questions.a: The Moon. It does not emit its own light; it only reflects the sunlight that falls on it.

questions.q: Match each object in Column I with its description in Column II. Column I: 1. The Sun 2. The Moon 3. A wax candle 4. An LED lamp. Column II: A. Does not emit light; reflects the light of the Sun B. Modern electric light source that uses much less power C. Natural source that emits its own light D. Artificial source that burns a fuel
questions.a: 1-C, 2-A, 3-D, 4-B: the Sun is a natural source that emits its own light, the Moon only reflects sunlight, a wax candle burns a fuel, and an LED lamp is an electric source using much less power.

questions.q: True or False: LED lamps use more power than traditional lamps, which is why they are brighter. Give the verdict and a reason.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the book says LED lamps consume much less power than traditional lamps, and are still brighter and last longer
questions.a: False. LED lamps consume much less power than traditional lamps, yet they are brighter and last longer.

questions.q: Answer briefly. (a) What is a luminous object? (b) Name two natural sources of light other than the Sun. (c) Name two fuels that humans used to make fire for light.
s: (a) An object that emits its own light
(b) Any two of: stars, lightning, natural fire, certain animals such as fireflies
(c) Any two of: animal fat, oil, wax, gas
questions.a: (a) A luminous object emits its own light. (b) Any two of stars, lightning, natural fire and animals such as fireflies. (c) Any two of animal fat, oil, wax and gas.

questions.q: Say whether each of the following is luminous or non-luminous, giving a one-line reason. (a) A firefly flashing at night (b) The Moon (c) A burning oil lamp (d) The planet Venus in the evening sky (e) A polished steel plate shining in sunlight
s: (a) Luminous: a firefly emits its own light
(b) Non-luminous: the Moon only reflects sunlight
(c) Luminous: the burning oil gives out its own light
(d) Non-luminous: objects of the solar system other than the Sun shine only by reflecting sunlight
(e) Non-luminous: the plate only reflects the sunlight falling on it
questions.a: (a) Luminous. (b) Non-luminous, it reflects sunlight. (c) Luminous, the flame emits light. (d) Non-luminous, Venus shines by reflecting sunlight. (e) Non-luminous, the plate only reflects sunlight.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Venus shines brightly in the evening sky, yet it is a non-luminous object. Reason (R): Objects in our solar system other than the Sun shine only by reflecting the light of the Sun. Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: Venus looks bright only because it reflects sunlight, so it is non-luminous.

questions.q: During a power cut at night, Meera's room has a burning candle, a glowing battery-run LED torch, a wall mirror showing the candle flame and a steel tumbler gleaming in the candlelight. How many of these four objects are luminous?
questions.a: Two: the burning candle and the glowing LED torch emit their own light; the mirror and the steel tumbler only reflect the candle's light.

questions.q: Ravi says, 'On a full-moon night I can read a newspaper by moonlight, so the Moon must be a luminous object.' (a) Is Ravi right? (b) Explain where moonlight comes from.
s: (a) No, the Moon is non-luminous; being bright does not mean it emits light
(b) Moonlight is sunlight that falls on the Moon and is reflected by it
questions.a: (a) No. Brightness alone does not make an object luminous; the Moon does not emit its own light. (b) Moonlight is the Sun's light reflected by the Moon.

questions.q: Nisha made this chart for her project. 'Natural sources of light: the Sun, the Moon, a firefly. Artificial sources of light: an oil lamp, lightning, an LED torch.' Her teacher gives 1 mark for each object placed correctly and 0 for each object placed wrongly. (a) Find each wrong entry and give the reason it is wrong. (b) Say where each wrong entry should go instead. (c) How many marks out of 6 does Nisha get?
s: (a) The Moon is wrong: it does not emit its own light and only reflects sunlight, so it is not a source of light at all
(a) Lightning is wrong: it is a natural source, not one made by humans
(b) The Moon goes in a list of non-luminous objects; lightning goes under natural sources
(c) The other four entries are correct, so she gets 4 out of 6
questions.a: The Moon is wrongly listed as a source: it is non-luminous and only reflects sunlight. Lightning is wrongly listed as artificial: it is a natural source. The Sun, the firefly, the oil lamp and the LED torch are placed correctly, so Nisha gets 4 marks out of 6.

questions.q: On a clear evening in a Western Ghats village, Jatin's grandfather points out five things in the sky to Keshav: the Moon rising over the hills, the planet Venus shining low in the west, a twinkling star, the flashing lamp of an aeroplane, and a flash of lightning from a far-off storm. Keshav wants to sort them. (a) Which of the five are luminous? (b) Which of the luminous ones are natural sources of light? (c) Among the luminous ones, which is an artificial source? (d) Jatin's grandfather adds that the fireflies flashing near the stream belong on the list too. Are they luminous or non-luminous, natural or artificial, and what do fireflies use their light for?
s: (a) The star, the aeroplane lamp and the lightning are luminous
(b) The star and the lightning are natural sources
(c) The aeroplane lamp is the artificial source
(d) Fireflies are luminous, natural sources of light (certain animals emit their own light); they use their light to communicate
questions.a: (a) The star, the aeroplane's lamp and the lightning. (b) The star and the lightning. (c) The aeroplane's lamp. (d) Fireflies are natural luminous sources, since they emit their own light, and they use it to communicate.

questions.q: In Activity 11.1 with three matchboxes, a torch and a screen, a bright spot appears on the screen only when:
o: The holes of all three matchboxes are in one straight line with the torch lamp
The middle matchbox is moved slightly to one side
The holes in the three matchboxes are at different heights
The torch is placed above the matchboxes
questions.a: All three holes are in one straight line with the torch lamp; light reaches the screen only along a straight path.

questions.q: We can see a candle flame through a straight pipe but not through the same pipe when it is bent. This shows that:
o: Light travels in a straight line
The flame goes out when the pipe is bent
Light can pass only through hollow objects
questions.a: Light travels in a straight line, so it cannot follow the bend in the pipe to reach the eye.

questions.q: True or False: A low-power laser pointer is safe to shine directly into a friend's eyes because it is low-power. Give the verdict and a reason.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: a laser beam must never be pointed at anyone's eyes, as it can cause serious eye damage; a laser is used only under a teacher's supervision
questions.a: False. Even a low-power laser must never be pointed directly at anyone's eyes, as it can cause serious eye damage; it is used only under a teacher's supervision.

questions.q: A laser beam is passed through a beaker of water. (a) Why is a drop of milk added to the water? (b) What kind of path does the beam follow inside the water?
s: (a) To make the laser beam easily visible
(b) A straight path
questions.a: (a) The drop of milk makes the beam easily visible. (b) The beam follows a straight path in the water.

questions.q: In Activity 11.1, answer the following. (a) What is placed on one side of the row of matchboxes? (b) What is placed on the other side? (c) What does the activity suggest about the way light travels?
s: (a) A torch, with its lamp at the height of the holes
(b) A cardboard screen
(c) Light travels in a straight line
questions.a: (a) A torch with its lamp at the height of the holes. (b) A cardboard screen. (c) It suggests that light travels in a straight line.

questions.q: Your class has three empty matchboxes, a pin, a torch, a sheet of cardboard and some books to raise the boxes. Write four steps you would follow to show that light travels in a straight line, ending with what you would observe.
s: Make a hole in the inner tray of each matchbox at exactly the same position
Arrange the three boxes in a straight line so that the holes are at the same height and in line
Place the torch on one side with its lamp at the height of the holes, and the cardboard screen on the other side
A bright spot is seen on the screen; when one box is moved slightly, the spot disappears, so light travels in a straight line
questions.a: Make holes at the same position in the three trays, line the boxes up with the holes at one height, place the torch at hole height on one side and the screen on the other. A spot appears on the screen and vanishes when any box is moved, showing light travels in a straight line.

questions.q: Consider the following statements. I. In the bent-pipe activity, light from the candle flame bends to follow the pipe, so the flame is still seen. II. In the matchbox activity, the torch is placed so that its lamp is at the height of the holes. III. The book says that light can sometimes bend around corners, which is learnt in higher grades. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only. Statement I is wrong: the flame is seen through a straight pipe but not through a bent pipe, which shows that light travels in a straight line.

questions.q: A carpenter checks whether a long wooden plank is straight by closing one eye and looking along its edge from one end. (a) Which property of light is he relying on? (b) If the plank bulges upward in the middle, why can he not see the far end of the edge? (c) Which activity of the chapter uses the same idea?
s: (a) Light travels in a straight line
(b) The bulge blocks the straight path of light from the far end to his eye, and light cannot go around it
(c) The matchbox activity or the straight and bent pipe activity
questions.a: (a) Light travels in a straight line. (b) The raised middle lies in the straight line from the far end to his eye and blocks that light. (c) The matchbox activity (or the bent-pipe activity) uses the same idea.

questions.q: Four friends look at a lighted candle (an adult is present) through flexible pipes. Pipe P is straight and points at the flame. Pipe Q is straight but points at the wall above the flame. Pipe R is bent in the middle. Pipe S is bent into a U shape. Through which pipe or pipes can the flame be seen?
questions.a: P only: light from the flame reaches the eye only along a straight pipe pointed at the flame; Q points elsewhere and R and S are bent.

questions.q: At a school science fair, Kiran shows the laser activity under his teacher's supervision with a low-power laser pointer. First he tries two beakers of water. Beaker P has clear water: visitors see only a red spot on the far side. Beaker Q has a drop of milk added: visitors see a thin red line across it. He then fills a glass tank 60 cm long with milky water and tilts the pointer, so the beam enters at the left wall 20 cm above the tank floor; 30 cm across the tank the red line is 15 cm above the floor. A friend offers him a high-power laser 'to make the line brighter'. (a) Which beaker should Kiran use to show visitors the path of the beam, and why? (b) How high above the floor will the red line be at the right wall, 60 cm across? (c) Did tilting the pointer change the shape of the path? What does this show? (d) Should Kiran accept the high-power laser? Give the reason from the book.
s: (a) Beaker Q: the drop of milk makes the laser beam easily visible, so its path can be seen
(b) 10 cm: the line drops 5 cm in the first 30 cm, so in a straight line it drops another 5 cm in the next 30 cm (20 - 5 - 5 = 10 cm)
(c) No: the beam is still a straight line, only sloping; light travels in a straight line whichever way it is aimed
(d) No: the book says to avoid high-power lasers for this activity; a low-power laser pointer is sufficient
questions.a: (a) Beaker Q, because the milk makes the beam easily visible. (b) 10 cm above the floor: the straight line falls 5 cm every 30 cm. (c) No; the path is still straight, only sloping, so light travels in a straight line in any direction. (d) No; the book says to avoid high-power lasers here, as a low-power pointer is sufficient.

questions.q: Five identical cards stand in a row between a torch and a screen, with their left edges lined up. Each card has one hole, and all holes are at the height of the torch lamp. The lamp is in line with a point 5 cm from the left edge of the cards. The table gives how far each hole is from the left edge of its card, from the card nearest the torch to the card nearest the screen. Set-up X: 5, 5, 5, 5, 5 cm. Set-up Y: 5, 5, 8, 5, 5 cm. Set-up Z: 5, 5, 5, 5, 3 cm. (a) In which set-up(s) will a bright spot appear on the screen? (b) Explain why there is no spot in set-up Y. (c) Explain why there is no spot in set-up Z. (d) In set-up Y, which card should be moved, which way and by how much, to get the spot? (e) Lalit says, 'In set-up Z the light passed four cards, so it must have stopped travelling straight at the fifth card.' Is he right?
s: (a) Only in set-up X, where all five holes and the lamp are in one straight line
(b) In Y the third hole (8 cm) is 3 cm out of line, so the solid part of the third card blocks the straight path of light
(c) In Z the light passes straight through the first four holes but meets the solid part of the fifth card (its hole is at 3 cm, 2 cm out of line), which blocks it
(d) Slide the third card 3 cm sideways towards the side where the left edges are lined up (to the left), so its hole comes to 5 cm from that line, in line with the others and the lamp
(e) No: the light still travels in a straight line; the fifth card's hole is out of line, so the card simply blocks it
questions.a: (a) Only set-up X. (b) In Y the third hole (8 cm) is 3 cm out of the straight line, so the third card blocks the light. (c) In Z the light goes straight through four holes but hits the solid part of the fifth card, whose hole (3 cm) is 2 cm out of line. (d) Slide the third card 3 cm towards the side of the lined-up left edges, so its hole comes to 5 cm from that line. (e) No; light keeps travelling straight and is simply blocked by the fifth card.

questions.q: A material through which light passes only partially is called:
questions.a: Translucent. Light passes partially through translucent materials.

questions.q: Match each item in Column I with the correct description in Column II. Column I: 1. Clear glass 2. Tracing paper 3. Cardboard 4. Shadow. Column II: A. Light does not pass through it B. Light passes almost completely through it C. The dark patch where light does not reach D. Light passes partially through it
questions.a: 1-B, 2-D, 3-A, 4-C: clear glass is transparent (light passes almost completely), tracing paper is translucent (light passes partially), cardboard is opaque (no light passes), and a shadow is the dark patch where light does not reach.

questions.q: True or False: A translucent object forms a darker shadow than an opaque object. Give the verdict and a reason.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: opaque objects form darker shadows; translucent objects make lighter shadows because some light passes through them
questions.a: False. Opaque objects form darker shadows; translucent objects let some light through and make lighter shadows.

questions.q: Shadow puppetry is part of our cultural heritage. Name any two regional styles of shadow puppetry along with the state each belongs to.
s: First correct style with its state, e.g. Tholu Bommalata (Andhra Pradesh)

Second correct style with its state, e.g. Togalu Gombeyaata (Karnataka), Ravana Chhaya (Odisha), Tholpavakoothu (Kerala), Bommalattam (Tamil Nadu), Charma Bahuli Natya (Maharashtra) or Keelu Bomme (Andhra Pradesh)
questions.a: Any two, for example Tholu Bommalata (Andhra Pradesh), Togalu Gombeyaata (Karnataka), Ravana Chhaya (Odisha), Tholpavakoothu (Kerala), Bommalattam (Tamil Nadu), Charma Bahuli Natya (Maharashtra) or Keelu Bomme (Andhra Pradesh).

questions.q: In Activity 11.4 an opaque object casts a shadow on a screen in torch light. What happens to the shadow when (a) the screen is removed, (b) the torch is switched off, (c) the colour of the object is changed?
s: (a) No shadow is seen, because there is no surface to act as a screen
(b) No shadow forms, because there is no source of light
(c) The shadow stays the same colour; changing the colour of an opaque object does not change the colour of its shadow
questions.a: (a) No shadow is seen without a screen. (b) No shadow forms without a light source. (c) The shadow's colour does not change.

questions.q: Assertion (A): In a closed room with no window and every lamp switched off, a chair casts no shadow on the floor. Reason (R): To observe a shadow we need a source of light, an opaque object and a screen. Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the chair and the floor are present, but with no source of light no shadow can form.

questions.q: At noon, Tara holds a glass of clear water, a sheet of tracing paper and a thick notebook, one beside the other, in sunlight above the ground. Which statement about their shadows on the ground is correct?
o: The notebook's shadow is the darkest, the tracing paper's is lighter, and the glass of water gives at most a faint shadow
All three give equally dark shadows because they all stand in sunlight
The glass of water gives the darkest shadow because it is the heaviest
The tracing paper gives no shadow at all, but the glass of water gives a dark one
questions.a: The notebook (opaque) gives the darkest shadow, the tracing paper (translucent) a lighter one, and the clear glass of water (transparent) at most a faint shadow.

questions.q: Class 7B in Bhopal repeats Activity 11.3 in a dark room with one torch and a white screen. The class records what reaches the screen for each object. Clear glass sheet: a bright spot, almost as bright as with nothing in the way. Tracing paper: a dim patch of light. Thick cardboard: no light, only a dark patch. Before the activity, Salma had predicted that tracing paper would let no light through. (a) Classify the three materials as transparent, translucent or opaque. (b) Salma's mother wants a lamp shade from one of these three that still lets some light into the room but hides the bright bulb. Which should she choose? (c) Was Salma's prediction correct? Give a reason from the data. (d) Why is the dark patch formed behind the cardboard?
s: (a) Clear glass: transparent; tracing paper: translucent; cardboard: opaque
(b) Tracing paper: it is translucent, so light passes partially through it (glass would not hide the bulb and cardboard would block all light)
(c) No: a dim patch reached the screen, so tracing paper lets light through partially
(d) Light travels in a straight line and the opaque cardboard blocks it, so light does not reach that part of the screen
questions.a: (a) Glass transparent, tracing paper translucent, cardboard opaque. (b) Tracing paper, since light passes partially through it. (c) No, the dim patch shows light passes partially through tracing paper. (d) The opaque cardboard blocks light travelling in a straight line, so that region gets no light: the shadow.

questions.q: Ramesh says, 'A shadow tells us everything about the object that makes it: its colour, its exact shape, and whether light can pass through it.' Judge each part of his claim using what you have learnt about shadows, and give your overall verdict.
s: Colour: wrong, because changing the colour of an opaque object does not change the colour of its shadow
Shape: not always; the shape of the shadow depends on the position of the object relative to the source and the screen, and sometimes we cannot guess the object at all
Light passing: partly right, since a dark shadow suggests an opaque object, a lighter one a translucent object and a faint one a transparent object
Overall: the claim is not correct; a shadow gives only some information about an object
questions.a: His claim is wrong. A shadow does not show colour, its shape changes with the positions of source, object and screen (we may not even guess the object), and only its darkness hints whether the object is opaque, translucent or transparent. A shadow gives some information, not everything.

questions.q: The change in the direction of light by a mirror is called:
questions.a: Reflection of light is the change in the direction of light by a mirror.

questions.q: A plane mirror is a mirror that is:
o: Able to emit its own light
questions.a: A plane mirror is flat and not curved.

questions.q: True or False: When a mirror redirects sunlight onto a wall, the light travels in a straight line up to the mirror and again in a straight line from the mirror to the wall. Give the verdict and a reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: light always travels in straight lines; it only changes direction where it falls on the mirror
questions.a: True. Light always travels in straight lines and changes direction only when it falls on the mirror.

questions.q: (a) How were mirrors made in earlier times, before glass mirrors? (b) Name the metal surface mirror that is still made in Kerala.
s: (a) By polishing stone or metal
(b) Aranmula Kannadi
questions.a: (a) Earlier mirrors were made by polishing stone or metal. (b) Aranmula Kannadi of Kerala.

questions.q: In Activity 11.6 a comb, a torch, white paper and a plane mirror are used. (a) Why are all openings of the comb except one closed with black paper? (b) What is seen on the white paper before the mirror is placed? (c) What happens to the beam after the mirror is placed in its path?
s: (a) To make a single thin slit so that a thin beam of light is obtained
(b) A thin beam of light along the paper
(c) The path of the beam changes at the mirror, that is, light is reflected
questions.a: (a) To leave one thin slit that gives a thin beam. (b) A thin beam of light along the paper. (c) The beam changes direction at the mirror: reflection of light.

questions.q: Morning sunlight comes in through a window and makes a bright patch on the floor. Neha wants a spot of light on the ceiling without moving anything else. What should she place in the sunlit patch?
o: A flat, shiny steel plate, tilted to face the ceiling
questions.a: A flat, shiny steel plate tilted towards the ceiling: a shiny surface changes the direction of light and sends a spot upward.

questions.q: Assertion (A): In Activity 11.6, the thin beam of light on the white paper changes its path after it falls on the plane mirror. Reason (R): The plane mirror is a luminous object that gives out a new beam of its own. Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: the beam changes its path because the mirror reflects the light falling on it; the mirror does not emit any light of its own, so it is non-luminous.

questions.q: At noon, Mohan wants to see the bottom of a deep, dark well in his courtyard. Sunlight falls on the courtyard floor but not into the well. (a) What can he use to send sunlight into the well? (b) How should he use it? (c) Name the two ideas of this chapter that explain why a bright spot reaches the bottom.
s: (a) A plane mirror or a shiny flat steel plate
(b) Hold it in the sunlight and tilt it until the spot of reflected light falls into the well
(c) Reflection: the mirror changes the direction of light; and light travels in a straight line from the mirror to the bottom
questions.a: (a) A plane mirror or shiny steel plate. (b) Hold it in sunlight and tilt it till the light spot goes down into the well. (c) Reflection of light by the mirror, and straight-line travel of light after reflection.

questions.q: The science club of a school in Kochi builds a cardboard maze with tall opaque walls. A torch is fixed at the entrance. From there the passage runs 40 cm straight ahead, turns right and runs 30 cm, then turns left and runs 20 cm to a paper target at the end. The club has two small plane mirrors on stands and a sheet of black chart paper. The room is dark, and the target must be lit by the torch alone. (a) Why does the torch beam not reach the target without any help? (b) How many mirrors are needed, and where should each be placed? (c) With both mirrors in place, the spot falls on the maze wall a little to one side of the target. What should the club do, and why does it work? (d) A member uses the black chart paper in place of the second mirror. Will the target be lit? Give a reason.
s: (a) Light travels in a straight line, so the beam goes straight ahead and is blocked by the opaque wall at the first turn
(b) Two mirrors: one at each turn, each tilted so that it sends the light along the next part of the passage
(c) Tilt the second mirror slightly; tilting a mirror changes the direction of the reflected light, so the spot moves onto the target
(d) No: the black chart paper is not shiny and does not redirect the light, so the light stops at the second turn
questions.a: (a) Light travels in straight lines, so the beam is blocked by the wall at the first turn. (b) Two plane mirrors, one at each turn, tilted to send the light along the next part of the passage. (c) Tilt the second mirror a little; tilting a mirror moves the reflected spot. (d) No; black chart paper is not a shiny surface, so it does not change the direction of the light towards the target.

questions.q: In a dark room a torch shines on a screen, and a wall stands on the opposite side. Meenal's partner holds four objects, W, X, Y and Z, one at a time in the torch beam, and Meenal records only what she sees. W: the screen stays brightly lit, with at most a faint shadow, and no spot on the wall. X: a dark shadow on the screen and a bright spot on the opposite wall. Y: a lighter shadow on the screen and no spot on the wall. Z: a dark shadow on the screen and no spot on the wall. The four objects are a clear glass sheet, tracing paper, a shiny flat steel plate and thick cardboard. (a) Which object is the steel plate? Give the evidence from the record. (b) Name the materials of W, Y and Z, giving a reason for each. (c) Meenal's partner tilts object X a little. What changes, and does the screen still show a shadow?
s: (a) X is the shiny steel plate: it is the only object that changes the direction of light to make a spot on the wall, and being opaque it also gives a dark shadow
(b) W is clear glass: light passes almost completely through it
(b) Y is tracing paper: light passes only partly, so the shadow is lighter
(b) Z is thick cardboard: it is opaque, giving a dark shadow, and it is not shiny, so it sends no spot to the wall
(c) The spot on the wall moves to a new position; the screen still shows a shadow because the steel plate still blocks the light
questions.a: (a) X, the only object that redirects light to the wall; it also blocks light, giving a shadow. (b) W is clear glass (light passes almost completely), Y is tracing paper (lighter shadow, light passes partly), Z is thick cardboard (opaque and not shiny: dark shadow, no wall spot). (c) The wall spot moves; the screen still shows a shadow as the steel plate is opaque.

questions.q: An upright image is called:
questions.a: An upright image is called erect.

questions.q: The word AMBULANCE is written laterally inverted on the front of an ambulance so that:
o: Drivers of vehicles ahead can read it correctly in their rear-view mirrors
Pedestrians on the footpath can read it directly
It reads correctly when seen upside down
It glows in the dark at night
questions.a: Drivers of the vehicles ahead read it correctly as AMBULANCE in their rear-view mirrors, because a plane mirror laterally inverts the image.

questions.q: Consider the following statements about the image formed by a plane mirror. I. It is of the same size as the object. II. It can be obtained on a screen placed behind the mirror. III. Its left and right appear swapped. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. The image is the same size as the object and is laterally inverted, but it cannot be obtained on a screen.

questions.q: True or False: When you walk closer to a plane mirror, your image also appears closer to the mirror. Give the verdict and a reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: in Activity 11.8 the image appears close to the mirror when we stand close to it and far when we stand far
questions.a: True. When you stand close to a plane mirror the image also appears close to it, and when you stand far it appears far.

questions.q: Priya combs her hair with a parting on the left side of her head and looks into a plane mirror. (a) Does her image seem to have the parting on its own left side or its own right side? (b) What is this left-right reversal called?
s: (a) On the image's own right side
(b) Lateral inversion
questions.a: (a) Her image seems to have the parting on its own right side. (b) This perceived left-right reversal is lateral inversion.

questions.q: The letters T and O look the same in a plane mirror because their left and right halves are alike. Using lateral inversion, which of these letters will look changed (reversed) in a plane mirror?
questions.a: F: its arms point only to the right, so in the laterally inverted image they point to the left. A, H and O have matching left and right halves and look unchanged.

questions.q: Assertion (A): When you raise your right arm in front of a plane mirror, your image seems to raise its left arm. Reason (R): The image formed by a plane mirror is erect. Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the left-right swap is due to lateral inversion, not to the image being erect.

questions.q: A tailor holds a 1 m long measuring tape hanging straight down in front of a large plane mirror, with the 0 cm end at the top. (a) How long does the image of the tape appear? (b) Is the 0 cm end at the top or the bottom of the image? Give a reason for each.
s: (a) 1 m long, because the image in a plane mirror is the same size as the object
(b) At the top, because the image in a plane mirror is erect
questions.a: (a) 1 m, since a plane mirror image is the same size as the object. (b) At the top, since the image is erect.

questions.q: Kavita wears a T-shirt with the number 25 printed on the front and stands in front of a plane mirror. (a) Will the number read 25 in the image? Explain. (b) Will the number look smaller when she steps back from the mirror? (c) Will the number appear upside down?
s: (a) No: because of lateral inversion left and right are swapped, so the 5 appears on the left and each digit is reversed
(b) No: the image is the same size as the object
(c) No: the image in a plane mirror is erect, not upside down
questions.a: (a) No; lateral inversion swaps left and right, so the digits appear in reverse order and each is reversed. (b) No, the image stays the same size. (c) No, the image is erect.

questions.q: At a science fair Anu is given two mirrors, A and B, that look alike from the front, and is told that only one of them is a plane mirror. She places a 12 cm long pen, tip up, in front of each and records: Mirror A: pen 10 cm away, image 12 cm long with the tip on top; pen 40 cm away, image 12 cm long with the tip on top; screen placed behind the mirror, no image. Mirror B: pen 10 cm away, image about 22 cm long with the tip on top; pen 40 cm away, image about 15 cm long with the tip at the bottom; screen placed behind the mirror, no image. (a) Which mirror is the plane mirror? (b) Give two pieces of evidence from her record. (c) Which of her tests does not help her decide, and why? (d) How long will the image of the pen in the plane mirror be when the pen is 25 cm away? Why?
s: (a) Mirror A is the plane mirror
(b) In A the image is 12 cm, the same size as the pen, at both distances; in B the size changes (about 22 cm and about 15 cm), so it is not the same size as the pen
(b) In A the image is erect at both distances; in B the tip appears at the bottom at 40 cm, so that image is upside down
(c) The screen test: neither mirror gave an image on a screen behind it, so it does not tell them apart
(d) 12 cm, because a plane mirror forms an image of the same size as the object at every position
questions.a: (a) Mirror A. (b) A's image is always 12 cm, the same size as the pen, and always erect; B's image changes size (about 22 cm, then about 15 cm) and is upside down at 40 cm, which a plane mirror never does. (c) The screen test does not help, as both mirrors gave no image on the screen behind them. (d) 12 cm, since a plane mirror image is the same size as the object.

questions.q: In Activity 11.9, the image of a candle flame formed on the screen through a small hole in a cardboard is:
o: Erect and exactly like the flame
questions.a: The image of the candle flame is upside down, that is, inverted.

questions.q: Match each device in Column I with its feature in Column II. Column I: 1. Pinhole camera 2. Periscope 3. Kaleidoscope 4. Plane mirror. Column II: A. Three mirror strips joined in a triangle give a new pattern on every turn B. Forms an erect, laterally inverted image that cannot be obtained on a screen C. Forms an inverted image on a screen through a tiny hole D. Two plane mirrors in a Z-shaped box show objects not directly visible
questions.a: 1-C, 2-D, 3-A, 4-B: the pinhole camera gives an inverted image on a screen, the periscope uses two mirrors in a Z-shaped box, the kaleidoscope uses three mirror strips in a triangle, and the plane mirror gives an erect, laterally inverted image.

questions.q: True or False: A kaleidoscope shows the same pattern every time it is turned. Give the verdict and a reason.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: one gets to see a different pattern every time the kaleidoscope is turned, because the three mirrors make multiple images by reflections of reflections
questions.a: False. A kaleidoscope shows a different pattern every time it is turned; its three mirrors form multiple images through reflections of reflections.

questions.q: Farhan's class in Lucknow builds the sliding pinhole camera of Activity 11.10 from two cardboard boxes, one of which slides into the other with very little gap. On one face of the larger box Farhan makes a small hole in the middle. On the opposite face of the smaller box he cuts a square of side about 5 cm and covers it with tracing paper. On a bright sunny morning he points the camera at the school's water tank tower across the ground and covers his head and the camera with a dark cloth. (a) What part of the camera is the tracing paper? (b) Which side of the smaller box should be inside the larger box? (c) What should Farhan do to make the image of the tower appear clearly? (d) Will the tower appear upright or upside down?
s: (a) The screen on which the image forms
(b) The side with the tracing paper
(c) Move the smaller box forward or backward until the image appears on the tracing paper
(d) Upside down (inverted)
questions.a: (a) The tracing paper is the screen. (b) The side with the tracing paper goes inside. (c) Slide the smaller box forward or backward until the image appears. (d) The tower appears upside down.

questions.q: Answer these questions about making a periscope and a kaleidoscope. (a) How many plane mirrors does a simple periscope use? (b) In what shape of box are they placed? (c) Give one place where periscopes are used. (d) How many mirror strips does a kaleidoscope have, and how are they joined? (e) Why does a kaleidoscope show many images of a few bangle pieces?
s: (a) Two plane mirrors
(b) A Z-shaped box
(c) Any one of: submarines, tanks, by soldiers to see outside their bunkers, to look ahead over taller friends
(d) Three rectangular mirror strips of equal width, joined in a triangle
(e) The three mirrors form multiple images by reflections of reflections
questions.a: (a) Two. (b) A Z-shaped box. (c) Submarines, tanks, soldiers in bunkers, or seeing over taller friends. (d) Three equal strips joined in a triangle. (e) Reflections of reflections in the three mirrors give multiple images.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The image formed by a pinhole camera is upside down, but the image formed by a plane mirror is not upside down. Reason (R): There is lateral inversion in the image formed by a plane mirror. Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: lateral inversion is a left-right swap and says nothing about why the pinhole image is upside down.

questions.q: Consider the following statements. I. A periscope lets us see objects that are not directly visible because of reflection from its two mirrors. II. A pinhole camera forms its image without using any mirror: light from the object passes through a tiny hole onto a screen. III. In the sliding pinhole camera, the screen is made of thin translucent paper such as tracing paper. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III. The periscope works by reflection from two mirrors, the pinhole camera uses only a tiny hole and a screen, and its screen is thin translucent paper such as tracing paper.

questions.q: A periscope has a mirror at the top and another at the bottom of a Z-shaped box. Trace the path of light from an object above a wall to the eye of a person standing behind the wall, and say why both mirrors are needed.
s: Light from the object travels in a straight line and falls on the top mirror (mirror 1), which changes its direction down the box
The light travels straight down the box to the bottom mirror (mirror 2), which changes its direction again towards the eye
Both are needed: the first turns light into the box and the second turns it out to the eye; reflection from two mirrors lets us see objects not directly visible
questions.a: Light from the object hits mirror 1 and is reflected down the box, travels straight to mirror 2 and is reflected into the eye. One mirror only sends the light down the box; the second is needed to send it out to the eye.

questions.q: Sana is making the sliding pinhole camera of Activity 11.10 and has run out of tracing paper for the screen. (a) Her brother suggests a piece of thick cardboard instead. Will she be able to see the image from the open side of the smaller box? Give a reason. (b) Her friend suggests a sheet of clear glass instead. Will it work as a screen? Give a reason.
s: (a) No: cardboard is opaque, so no light passes through it and she cannot see any image from the open side
(b) No: light passes almost completely through clear glass, so the image is not caught on it; a translucent sheet that lets light pass partly is needed
questions.a: (a) No; opaque cardboard lets no light through, so nothing is seen from the open side. (b) No; clear glass lets light pass almost completely, so it does not hold the image; the screen must be translucent, like tracing paper.

questions.q: Four groups build the sliding pinhole camera of Activity 11.10 and test it on the same sunlit school building, each covering head and camera with a dark cloth. Group P: pinhole facing the building, tracing-paper screen, smaller box slid until the image appeared: they see a clear picture. Group Q: same camera as P, but they hold the open side towards the building and look in through the pinhole: they see no picture of the building. Group R: covered the square opening of the smaller box with thick cardboard instead of tracing paper, pinhole facing the building: they see nothing on the screen. Group S: camera made exactly like P's and pointed correctly, but the boxes were never slid: the screen shows only a blur. (a) What does Group P see, the right way up or upside down? (b) What is wrong with Group Q's method? (c) Why does Group R see nothing, and what must they use instead? (d) What should Group S do?
s: (a) An inverted (upside down) image of the building on the tracing paper

(b) The pinhole must face the object and they must look through the open side of the smaller box; held the other way, light from the building does not pass through the pinhole to form an image on the screen
(c) Cardboard is opaque, so light that comes through the pinhole cannot pass through it and nothing is seen from behind
(c) They must use thin translucent paper such as tracing paper, through which light passes partially, so the image can be seen from behind
(d) Move the smaller box forward or backward until the image appears clearly on the tracing paper
questions.a: (a) An upside-down (inverted) image of the building. (b) They held it the wrong way: the pinhole must face the building and they must look through the open side. (c) Cardboard is opaque and lets no light through, so nothing shows from behind; a thin translucent screen such as tracing paper is needed. (d) Slide the smaller box forward or backward until the image appears on the tracing paper.

questions.q: Rohan has a Z-shaped box to look over a wall, but only one plane mirror. He fixes it at the top bend, facing the scene beyond the wall and slanting down the box. When he looks into the lower opening he sees only the dark inside of the box. Explain why he sees nothing of the scene and what he must add to make the periscope work.
s: The top mirror reflects light from the scene and turns it down the box
Light travels in a straight line down the box and falls on the opaque cardboard wall at the lower bend, which does not turn it towards his eye
He must fix a second plane mirror at the lower bend, facing the top mirror, slanted so it turns the light out through the lower opening to his eye
With reflection from the two mirrors, light from the scene reaches his eye, so he sees objects that are not directly visible
questions.a: With one mirror the light from the scene is turned down the box but then travels straight into the cardboard wall at the lower bend, so none reaches his eye. A second plane mirror at the lower bend, facing the top mirror, turns the light out to his eye; reflection from two mirrors lets him see over the wall.
